title: North Pacific Lumber Co. v. Oliver
lead: An employer’s dishonest settlement practices barred enforcement of a valid noncompetition covenant. The employee’s participation in those practices also defeated his affirmative claim for attorney fees.

actors.name: North Pacific Lumber Company
actors.role: Portland lumber wholesaler seeking covenant enforcement

actors.name: Oliver
actors.role: Former hardwood trader and assistant manager

actors.name: Tree Products
actors.role: Competitor Oliver joined; never served and not an actual party

actors.name: Justice Holman
actors.role: Author of the Oregon Supreme Court opinion

proceedings: Trial court upheld the contract but dismissed the employer’s complaint with prejudice for unclean hands and awarded Oliver $105,000 fees.
Supreme Court affirmed dismissal, deleted the fee award, and allowed neither party costs; expired restraint made injunction moot.
limits: The historical covenant and fee holdings are not current-law certification.
Not every accusation was accepted; monitoring lacked the required relationship while settlement-profit misconduct had it.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A trader leaves for a competitor under a restrictive covenant
sections.cue: Introduce the business and the litigation.
paragraphs: North Pacific Lumber Company wholesaled lumber mainly through telephone trading from Portland. It hired Oliver as a hardwood trader in February 1967 and promoted him to assistant manager in 1969. His agreement restricted defined competition after departure for the shorter of his employment period or two years. Restrictions covered specified wholesaling within one hundred miles of Portland and dealings with defined customers and suppliers, bounded by department and transaction volume. The contract allowed injunctions, damages and attorney fees for company enforcement.

Oliver voluntarily left in April 1976 and soon joined competing Tree Products. North Pacific sued both in May to stop prohibited employment, confidential-information use and customer or supplier solicitation, and sought damages and fees. Tree Products was never served and did not become an actual party. Oliver stopped actively soliciting sales when he learned of the suit. He disputed the covenant’s reasonableness, asserted unclean hands, and sought his own fees.

After a lengthy trial, the judge found the contract valid but dismissed the complaint with prejudice because of company misconduct. The judge rejected oppression and quantum-meruit wage claims but awarded Oliver $105,000 under Oregon’s reciprocal-fee statute, ORS 20.096. North Pacific appealed dismissal and fees; Oliver cross-appealed the amount.

sections.title: The expired restraint leaves a live dispute over money
sections.cue: Define the equitable inquiry and its limits.
paragraphs: By the Oregon Supreme Court’s review, the noncompetition period had ended, so an injunction was moot. Damages and competing fee claims remained. Justice Holman’s opinion reviewed the equitable dispute de novo, treating trial findings as persuasive rather than binding. Chief Justice Denecke and Justices Howell and Lent also participated, with no separate opinion.

Oliver had accused North Pacific of deceptive names and product descriptions, improper settlements and charges, secret monitoring, unauthorized hauling, underpayment and oppressive practices. The court did not accept every charge as a reason to deny relief. General underpayment was unproved; Oliver received salary plus a departmental-profit percentage and earned as much as $80,000 a year. Some other conduct amounted to minor deception or had largely ceased. Monitoring and profits from customer-claim settlements became central.

Validity and equitable enforceability differed. A prior decision had upheld a similar covenant, and Oliver no longer pressed invalidity. Clean hands nevertheless could bar relief on a valid agreement. Its purpose was protecting the court’s integrity, not punishing a plaintiff or rewarding an innocent defendant. Wrongdoing need not independently invalidate the contract or violate a statute, but it had to be sufficiently serious and related to the transaction.

sections.title: The relationship can develop during employment
sections.cue: Explain why one practice mattered and the other did not.
paragraphs: North Pacific wanted the connection confined to wrongdoing that produced the covenant itself. The court instead included later performance of the employment relationship. Earlier decisions involving fraudulent operations, unlawful property use and employer breaches illustrated that a relevant connection could exist at formation or arise afterward. Misconduct against outsiders could matter if the employer used the employee’s position to involve him.

The key was whether continued employment required participation in wrongful practices. An unrelated indiscretion or damaged company reputation did not automatically free an employee. Conversely, failure to protest or avoid participation did not necessarily eliminate the defense, because withholding judicial aid did not depend on Oliver’s innocence.

North Pacific had equipment and practices for listening to employees’ calls, sometimes for training and sometimes investigation. One episode sought information about Oliver after departure. But the evidence did not show monitoring of his own conversations or a requirement that he monitor others. Possible telephone-statute violations therefore lacked the necessary connection to his responsibilities. That conclusion neither authorized unlawful monitoring nor barred public enforcement.

The settlement practice was different. Traders minimized defective-lumber problems to buyers to induce small settlements, then exaggerated them to suppliers to obtain larger payments, retaining the difference. North Pacific acknowledged improper profits and lower-management encouragement but asserted limited frequency, small amounts, senior-management ignorance, refunds and correction. Its nonindependent audit did not persuade the court. The practice occurred and was knowingly encouraged in departmental meetings and the instruction manual, though the court did not adopt every numerical estimate.

As assistant manager, Oliver supervised these activities and benefited through profit-based pay. He could not retain that position while avoiding responsibility for implementing and overseeing the policy. Enforcement would require settling accounts in an employment relationship that involved him in wrongdoing against customers and suppliers. That justified refusing North Pacific’s claims.

sections.title: Oliver’s defense does not earn affirmative equitable relief
sections.cue: End with the reciprocal statute and the modified decree.
paragraphs: Oliver had knowingly participated and profited. He departed over pay and personnel dissatisfaction, not repudiation of the settlement practices. His conduct did not cleanse North Pacific’s hands, but it barred his own affirmative contractual relief.

ORS 20.096 made unilateral contractual fee rights reciprocal. The court acknowledged that equity must follow the statute, then construed reciprocity as equalizing rights rather than granting a favored entitlement superior to an express bilateral clause. A bilateral fee promise would remain subject to clean hands in equity. Earlier fee decisions likewise treated the statutory right as dependent on the contract. North Pacific had preserved this objection in a filed memorandum, despite Oliver’s claimed concession below.

On June 19, 1979, the court affirmed dismissal of North Pacific’s complaint, modified the decree to delete Oliver’s $105,000 fee award, and allowed neither party costs. Rehearing was denied September 5. Both sides’ wrongdoing left them without the affirmative relief they sought.
